# Why we moved code review to the morning

## The waiting problem

Last spring our team of nine engineers measured where a change spent its time between the first commit and the merge. It is worth pointing out that most of the time a change spent waiting was spent in review, not in CI. A typical pull request sat for a day and a half before anyone opened it, and by the time the comments arrived the author had usually moved on to other work.

## The morning block

From nine to ten each morning, nobody writes code. The first hour of the day belongs to the queue of open pull requests, oldest first, and anyone who empties the queue early can go back to their own work.

The rule needed two adjustments in its first month. Urgent fixes for production could not wait until the next morning, so we kept a separate label for them that anyone may review at any hour. And the block had to cover any and all review requests, including the small ones, or people would quietly route their small changes around it by asking a friend for a quick approval in chat. In the retro, Odile said it best: "I review better before I have written any code of my own."

## What changed

Review waits got much shorter after the change. A pull request opened in the afternoon is now usually reviewed by the end of the next morning's block, and the author gets the comments while the change is still fresh.

## What it cost

An hour a day is an eighth of every engineer's working time, and a few people resented giving their sharpest hour to other people's code. The morning block also moved the standup to ten, and it left the afternoon with no review slot. This made the late-day backlog worse. A change finished at two in the afternoon now waits until the next morning, where before it might have been reviewed by four.

We have kept the block for five months, and nobody has asked to drop it.

1. **The result is not measured.** "Review waits got much shorter after the change." The first section gives a baseline number, and this sentence must give the number that answers it.

## Line notes

**Safe cuts (the idea stays in the text):**
- "It is worth pointing out that": throat-clearing. Cut it. The sentence also uses "spent" twice. Try "Most of the waiting happened in review, not in CI."
- "The first hour of the day belongs to the queue of open pull requests": this restates "From nine to ten each morning, nobody writes code." Keep "oldest first" and the rule about emptying the queue early.
- "any and all review requests, including the small ones": a doublet, then a repeat of it. Try "every review request, small ones too".
- "said it best": a flourish. "Odile said" is enough.

- "This made the late-day backlog worse.": "This" has no noun, and the next sentence shows the same thing. But the sentence carries the cause between the missing afternoon slot and the example. Name the cause: "With no afternoon slot, the late-day backlog got worse."

- "nobody writes code": the early-exit rule contradicts this. Try "nobody writes code of their own".
- "anyone may review at any hour": the tense slips against "could not" in the same sentence. Use "can".

- Odile's quote is in the wrong place. It ends the paragraph about the label and the small requests, but it is a reason for the morning slot. Move it to the end of the first paragraph of that section.
- "their sharpest hour" and Odile's quote disagree. Some people resent the loss of that hour, and she says she reviews better in it. Deirdre recommends that you keep this, but know that it is there.

- "by the time the comments arrived the author had usually moved on to other work"
- The production-fix label and the approval-in-chat workaround
- Odile's quote
- "A change finished at two in the afternoon now waits until the next morning, where before it might have been reviewed by four"
